newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Official says Russia army reform will be painful.
newsitem.headline: Official says Russia army reform will be painful.

text.p: A Russian senior official said on Saturday that military reform, forced on Moscow through the failure of a struggling national budget to maintain its huge Soviet-era armed forces, will be painful and cannot be rushed.

The secretary of the newly-established Defence Council, Yuri Baturin, told a news conference that the body, which met for the first time on Friday, would spearhead the reform. "So far the process of change has not been effective enough," Baturin said.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, chairing Friday's meeting in the absence of hospital-bound President Boris Yeltsin, said painful steps had to go ahead quickly.
Baturin quoted Chernomyrdin as saying that "concrete, real and unpopular measures" must be taken promptly.
A chronic cash shortage and a lack of clarity about future prospects have caused discontent among much of the military.
Russian security chief Alexander Lebed said last week that the army could be hit by revolts as a result of unpaid wages.
Baturin said he did not believe in the possibility of mutiny unless it were deliberately provoked.
"The military generally stick to discipline," he said.
Baturin said that the Kremlin was being forced into military reform without having a proper defence doctrine.
After Friday's Defence Council, Baturin said one of the difficulties facing the reform process was uncertainty over plans by NATO to expand into eastern Europe.
Lebed, making his first trip to the West, will visit NATO headquarters in Brussels on Monday and Tuesday.
In comments to the German magazine Der Spiegel, released on Saturday, Lebed accused the western alliance of failing to adapt to the realities of the post-Cold War era.

"The threat supposedly posed by the Soviet Union and the Warsaw pact five or ten years ago no longer exists," the outspoken general said. "But NATO formulates and realises its aims and tasks just as it did before."
Baturin was sceptical about a plan to turn the army into a purely professional force and end conscription by 2000. Yeltsin made the pledge in his reelection campaign this spring.

"I rather share the opinion of the defence minister that this can be done by 2005," Baturin said. "In general I'd like someone to tell me what the Russian economy will look like in two years before making such far-reaching predictions."
Baturin said he was much more worried by prospects of the best officers leaving the army in despair of improvement.
He said that the military reform was aimed at creating armed forces that would be both effective and affordable.
"The main task is to maintain the capability of the armed forces to fight," Baturin said. "But the state must be able to afford any such solution financially."
The Defence Council meeting examined ways of reorganising the armed forces. Government officials said there were too many generals and too much bureaucracy.
Some changes have already been made.
The Defence Ministry said on Friday Yeltsin sacked several senior generals and Russian media said the move showed Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, appointed in July, was ready for action.

Rodionov has announced plans to reduce the army to 1.2 million from about 1.5 million men. Baturin said the least effective units would be disbanded but he was worried that the ranks could be thinned badly as a result of the cash squeeze.
